ig_carousel_topic.topic: The Kelly criterion — explained without the math degree
ig_carousel_topic.slide1_text: Why betting the same amount every game is quietly costing you money
ig_carousel_topic.slide2_text:
Most bettors use flat stakes — 1 unit, every game, no matter what.
The problem: not every edge is equal.
A 54% edge and a 62% edge shouldn't get the same bet.
ig_carousel_topic.slide3_text:
Kelly says: size your bet to match your edge.
Bigger edge → bigger bet. Smaller edge → smaller bet.
The formula scales your stake to the actual probability you've identified — not your gut.
ig_carousel_topic.slide4_text:
Simple example:
You think a team has a 57% chance to win. The book implies 50%.
Full Kelly says bet about 14% of your bankroll.
Most sharps use Half Kelly (7%) to cushion variance.
Small edge = small bet. That's the point.
ig_carousel_topic.slide5_text:
You don't need a math degree — you need the discipline to bet less when the edge is thin.
Kelly doesn't guarantee wins. It helps you survive the losing stretches long enough to let your edge play out.
Save this one.
